title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (n=300 tasks) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) intervention increases the fraction of validator‑passing vendor‑specific CLI configurations produced from operator intent, relative to direct LLM generation. Tasks were a curated multi‑vendor (Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) intent manifest; a deterministic validator encoded syntactic, interface‑assignment, basic routing‑reachability, and destructive‑pattern checks; and the model was declared as gpt-5-mini. Per the preregistered paired design a single initial candidate was generated per task and shared between the baseline (no repair) and guarded (validate + single automatic repair if validator fails) arms. Across 300 paired tasks every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator (baseline = 300/300, guarded = 300/300; n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.00, 0.00]). All raw outputs, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, task manifest, and analysis artifacts are published and hash‑signed. We discuss interpretation (ceiling effect, validator coverage, model/prompt regimes), operational implications, reproducible follow‑ups, and the study’s limitations.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are proposed for intent→configuration translation and other NetOps tasks, but operators deploy validators and repair loops to reduce operational risk. Prior work has proposed generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) and tool‑assisted pipelines; however, quantitative preregistered evidence measuring the marginal safety benefit of a G‑V‑R pipeline for vendor CLI synthesis remains limited. We ask: to what extent does a deterministic‑validator‑centered G‑V‑R pipeline increase the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI fragment passes operational validation, compared with direct LLM generation? We contribute (1) a machine‑readable preregistration and a curated 300‑task multi‑vendor manifest; (2) a deterministic, operationally motivated validator and a paired confirmatory run using gpt-5-mini under a shared‑initial‑candidate protocol; (3) full artifact publication and a transparent analysis showing no measurable G‑V‑R benefit for this manifest and model snapshot, plus discussion and reproducibility artifacts.
sections.related_work: Work on LLM→NetOps and intent‑driven configuration includes studies on fine‑tuning, in‑context learning, RAG, and intent translation (e.g., Nguyen Tu et al., 2024; Chakraborty et al., 2024; Mondal et al., 2025). Benchmarks such as NetLLMBench emphasize validator design. Formal verification and SMT approaches for BGP/policy verification motivate deterministic validators (Weitz et al., 2016). Surveys of AIOps/agentic NetOps highlight the need for reproducible evaluations of safety mechanisms. Our study performs a tightly preregistered, artifact‑anchored confirmatory test of the marginal safety contribution of a bounded G‑V‑R policy.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. We preregistered study_id study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6. Design: paired binary outcomes on 300 tasks; for each task one initial candidate was generated and shared between arms. Baseline: validator(initial_candidate). Guarded: validator(initial_candidate) OR validator(repair_candidate) if initial fails (single automatic repair allowed). Task manifest. The curated 300‑task manifest (multi‑vendor: Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista) and vendor assignments, canonicalization rules, and full task payloads are recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (artifact SHA‑256: 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Model and prompts. Declared model snapshot: gpt-5-mini (see execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). The vendor adapter prompt templates, repair prompt template, and canonicalization logic are included in the published Docker artifact (execution/model_configuration.json and provider trace files). Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces vendor‑specific syntactic parsing, interface assignment invariants, workflow ordering constraints (e.g., shut→modify→restore patterns), forbidden destructive patterns (e.g., taking both uplinks down), and simple reachability invariants; it is deterministic and rule‑based (validator code and rules are published with the artifact bundle). Execution. Per preregistration we generated a single initial candidate per task (shared). Baseline outcome: validator(initial). Guarded outcome: validator(initial) or validator(repair) if validator(initial) fails. All calls, seeds, raw outputs, provider traces, and validator traces were logged and hash‑signed. Analysis. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided; 95% CI via paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Secondary analyses: pre‑specified per‑vendor paired tests (Bonferroni adjustment) and exploratory repair diagnostics (repair success conditional on initial failure). Missingness/contamination. A preregistered retry policy handled transient provider failures; contamination detection ran (exact/fuzzy match and high‑entropy token heuristics) and is logged (analysis/contamination_summary.csv).

sections.discussion: Interpretation. The preregistered paired test observed a ceiling effect: the initial generator (given the declared prompt and model snapshot) produced validator‑passing vendor CLI fragments for every curated task, so the bounded G‑V‑R intervention (single automatic repair) could not improve a zero‑discordance outcome. This null result should not be read as a universal claim that guarded pipelines are unnecessary; rather, it shows the marginal utility of a guarded repair depends on (a) the generator’s quality under the chosen prompt/model snapshot, (b) validator expressiveness, and (c) task difficulty and distribution. Practical implications. Guarded G‑V‑R pipelines remain operationally useful when initial generations fail deterministic checks or when validators encompass richer dynamic/simulation checks; they also provide auditable repair traces and an explicit safety budget. Reproducible next steps. To empirically measure G‑V‑R benefit one should (i) increase task difficulty / inject adversarial/out‑of‑distribution intents to produce nontrivial initial failure rates, (ii) expand the validator to include simulation/emulation (stateful execution, Batfish‑style checks) and deeper routing invariants, (iii) evaluate multiple model snapshots and model families, and (iv) consider bounded iterative repair policies rather than a single repair attempt. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial‑candidate design (preregistered) intentionally fixes the starting candidate to isolate the repair effect; because baseline initial candidates all passed the validator (n11=300), no repair calls occurred. Construct validity: our deterministic validator operationalizes a conservative subset of 'non‑harmful' properties and omits dynamic/timing hazards. External validity: single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) and the curated 300‑task manifest limit generalizability. Conclusion validity: the observed perfect baseline outcome produces exact inference (p=1.00) but precludes evidence that a G‑V‑R policy would help under other generator/validator/task regimes.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to quantify the marginal safety benefit of a bounded G‑V‑R pipeline for vendor CLI synthesis. Under the declared prompt, model snapshot (gpt-5-mini), and curated 300‑task manifest, the initial generations passed the deterministic validator in every case; thus the guarded single‑repair policy provided no measurable improvement. The result highlights that the practical benefit of guarded repair depends on generator error rates and validator fidelity. We publish all artifacts (task manifest, validator code, provider traces, raw outputs, and analysis) to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, validator scope, and model family to map the operational regimes where G‑V‑R meaningfully reduces risk.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic, interface invariants, workflow ordering, forbidden destructive patterns) and omits dynamic/simulation checks and deep routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or real‑world out‑of‑distribution failure modes; manifest design produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements.

Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) intentionally fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect, which prevents measuring generation variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; multi‑iteration repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; flagged samples would be handled per preregistered rules (no flagged pairs were observed).
